catalog_quote: Klemtoon. I. De klemtoon valt op de voorlaatste lettergreep. a. bij tweelettergrepige woorden van Tobel. oorsprong. Afwijkend van dezen regel zijn de twee of meerlettergrepige woorden die in de laatste lettergreep een tweeklank hebben, b.v.b.: bakau, nonau, ruae, bidilou e.a. De lettergreep met den tweeklank heeft den klemtoon, omdat die tweeklank oorspronkelijk bestaan heeft uit twee afzonderlijke klanken, waarvan natuurlijk de eerste den klemtoon had ... Bij deze woorden valt dus de klemtoon op den laatsten lettergreep. Hetzelfde geldt voor woorden die eindigen op een langen saamgetrokken klank, als damā, tiri e.a. ... b. audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim in the held PDF/scanned/page images of Hueting 1936 at BKI 94 pp. 324-325 (PDF 378-379), and the p.297 supporting remark is also there; the record's paraphrase of rules I-V and the two-domain suffix statement is faithful. (2) The classification rests on a 1936 Dutch missionary grammar sketch with an explicit stress chapter — first-hand and specific, so nothing suggests it is wrong, but it is 90 years old, impressionistic, and its weight clause is the author's historical rationalisation of diphthongs as contracted V+V. The one modern grammar (Holton 2003, Lincom, 99 pp) is not held and not open; no phonology article or instrumental study of Tobelo appears in Glottolog 5.1 (28 entries scanned) or on the WALS page, and WALS/StressTyp2 themselves rest on Hueting 1908/1936. sources.note: Hueting 1936 p.297 says his Woordenboek marked the relevant vowels with a grave accent, so the dictionary gives stress-marked headwords en masse; it is the second source WALS 14A and StressTyp2 cite for Tobelo and would let us test rule I.a (final diphthong/long vowel) and rule II (antepenult class) on hundreds of words instead of the 20 in the sketch.

sources.note: Only modern grammar of Tobelo (Glottolog hhtype 'grammar'); its phonology section (inventory + syllable structure per Lincom blurb) would settle whether final 'diphthongs'/long vowels are heavy syllables or V.V sequences, i.e. whether our weight-hedged (CVV) coding should stand or become plain penultimate; our record rests solely on a 1936 missionary sketch and its own examples fit the formalized rule only 15/20.
